name: A smudged ticker tape
brief:
An old ticker codes letters as numbers: A is 1, B is 2, and so on up to Z as 26. A tape is a run of these codes with no gaps. No code starts with 0, so `0` alone and `05` are not codes. Some digits are smudged and shown as `?`, and each could be any digit from 0 to 9. Count the letter messages each tape could hold, over every way of reading the smudges. The input comes as one string.

- The first line holds `t`, the number of tapes.
- Each of the next `t` lines holds one tape of digits and `?`.

Write `solve_tape_decodes(text)`, which returns the counts modulo `1_000_000_007`, one per line in the order of the tapes.

Example. The tape `1?` reads as 1 and then one of 1 to 9, which is 9 messages, or as one code from 10 to 19, which is 10 more. The tape `?0` can only be 10 or 20. For these two tapes the answer is `'19\n2'`.
constraints: $1 \le t \le 1{,}000$ tapes of 1 or more characters, at most 200,000 characters in all. Lines may carry extra spaces, and the text may end with blank lines.
$O(\text{total length})$ time is the target. Plain recursion over the ways to cut a tape is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Let `count[i]` be the messages for the first `i` characters. The last character alone adds `count[i - 1]` times the codes it can be, and the last two together add `count[i - 2]` times the codes from 10 to 26 they can be.

examples.note: `1?` gives 9 two-letter messages and 10 one-letter ones. `?0` is 10 or 20, since `0` alone is no code.
Read as two codes there are 9 messages; as one code only 17 fits, since 27 is past Z.

tests.call:
solve_tape_decodes('1000
' + '
'.join(''.join('12?7?0'[(i * j + j * j) % 6] for j in range(1, 200)) for i in range(1000)) + '
')

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method is plain recursion that reads one or two characters and recurses on the rest, which branches at every smudge and runs out of time on the long tapes. The step to the target is a running pair of counts, `count[i - 2]` and `count[i - 1]`, with each pair of characters priced by how many codes it can be. Unlike the well-known version, where a smudge is 1 to 9, here it may also be 0, so `1?` makes 10 codes, `2?` makes 7 and `??` makes 17.
notes: Each message ends in a one-digit or a two-digit code, so the count for `i` characters comes from the counts for `i - 1` and `i - 2`.
A smudge alone is 9 codes because 0 is not a code, but in a pair it may be 0, as in 10 and 20.
Each character is priced once with a fixed rule, so the work is $O(\text{total length})$.

planted.slip: Letting a smudge stand only for 1 to 9 in a pair, as in the well-known version, drops the codes 10 and 20.
Counting two codes for a smudge before any digit forgets that 27, 28 and 29 are past Z.
Plain recursion over every reading is right but branches at each smudge and repeats the same tails, too slow.
